title: A World Statistical Atlas of Continental Border Fractal Dimensions: Series Part II
content: This study extends fractal boundary analysis from national borders to continental and subcontinental landmasses through a 29-unit hierarchical framework comprising six continents and 23 subcontinents, defined under a modified UN M49 structure with study-specific connectivity rules. Each geographical unit was constructed and measured directly from its external perimeter, so parent-continent estimates represent distinct boundary geometries rather than averages or weighted combinations of constituent subcontinental dimensions. Adaptive box-counting (BC) and divider (DIV) estimators were applied under a common finite-scale procedure, followed by descriptive scale-stratified analysis of boundary complexity, parent–subcontinent contrasts, cross-method correspondence, method sensitivity, and equal-weight consensus fractal dimensions (FDs). Continental mean FDs exceeded subcontinental means under both methods (BC: 1.160842 vs. 1.136353; DIV: 1.172651 vs. 1.141075). Cross-method agreement was strong at both scales (continents: Pearson r = 0.9876, Lin CCC = 0.9624; subcontinents: Pearson r = 0.9822, Lin CCC = 0.9743). Greenland and Northern Europe occupied the upper end of the hierarchy, whereas Southern Africa formed the lower extreme. Despite this overall agreement, substantial within-family heterogeneity and localized method-sensitive differences remained. The resulting Continental Atlas provides a reproducible hierarchical framework for characterizing macro- scale boundary complexity while preserving geographical scale, direct perimeter construction, and estimator-specific information.
